Even before loading the data, based on the introduction we can safely assume that they had to conduct tests in colder weathers and not rely in scenarios they think are "reliable".

Loading data
```{r}
data = read.csv("shuttle.csv",header=T)
data
```
First impression looking at the samples, I think there were way too little tests conducted. I get it that it would be costlier, but I don't think safety has a price. Analyzing more into it, why it took them few years to change the pressure? Maybe it was still under development but why not tweak it just a bit? Also, but take it just as a guess, for around 70F degrees (about 21C), the sweet spot is at 100psi.

```{r}
data = data[data$Malfunction>0,]
data
```
After filtering the data only to show the malfunction, keeping in mind what was said earlier, there is my observation: you can't have any certain conclusion based on this little samples. First of all, 23 samples are not enough tests and having only 7 malfunctions doesn't really get you enough information. Second of all, the pressure for all the malfunctions is pretty much 200psi (one exception) which again is not enough to conclude something (if we look at the temperature it doesn't matter if it is colder or hotter but yet again you can't have something certain from this).
Therefore, the conclusion is that discarding the tests without malfunctions biases the dataset and the analysis is not right.

How does the frequency of failure vary with temperature?
```{r}
plot(data=data, Malfunction/Count ~ Temperature, ylim=c(0,1))
```
Frequency isn't impacted directly by the temperature.
We can try to estimate the impact of the temperature on the probability of O-ring malfunction.
```{r}
logistic_reg = glm(data=data, Malfunction/Count ~ Temperature, weights=Count, 
                   family=binomial(link='logit'))
summary(logistic_reg)
```
The most likely estimator of the temperature parameter is 0.0014 and the standard error of this estimator is 0.122, in other words we cannot distinguish any particular impact and we must take our estimates with caution.

The expectation for that day was 31F. Let's see the prediction of the malfunction.
```{r}
# shuttle=shuttle[shuttle$r!=0,] 
tempv = seq(from=30, to=90, by = .5)
rmv <- predict(logistic_reg,list(Temperature=tempv),type="response")
plot(tempv,rmv,type="l",ylim=c(0,1))
points(data=data, Malfunction/Count ~ Temperature)
```
It looks like the probability stays at 0.2 but as concluded previously, this prediction doesn't really make sense. I think that another problem was not only the lack of data but the arrogance and not taking the responsibility for not having enough data.
Anyway, this is how the prediction should have looked like:
```{r}
# shuttle=shuttle[shuttle$r!=0,] 
logistic_reg <- glm(cbind(Malfunction, Count - Malfunction) ~ Temperature, 
                    data = data, 
                    family = binomial)
tempv <- seq(from = 0, to = 90, by = 0.5)
rmv <- predict(logistic_reg, list(Temperature = tempv), type = "response")
plot(tempv, rmv, type = "l", ylim = c(0, 1), xlim = c(0, 90),
     xlab = "Temperature", ylab = "Probability")
points(Malfunction / Count ~ Temperature, data = data)
abline(v = 31, col = "red", lty = 2)
```
PS: when knitting, the graph is not correctly drawn (loading data set conflicts maybe) I will attach a screenshot of it separately. 
As we can see with the all data set included, the chances of malfunction are higher at lower temperatures. The red-line represents the expected 31F temperature. We can see that the probability is pretty high, therefore the logic of the previous graph is no longer valid. 

Last conclusion: the dataset didn't even include the 31F temperature, the lowest they had was 53F with 2 malfunctions, resulting in an unprecise analysis.
